Subject: Post-call recap: p95/p99 latency targets + next steps

Hi Emma / Raj —

Thanks for taking the time today. Quick recap and proposed next steps so we stay aligned on the SLO qualification: 

Call highlights:
- FinLytics target: p95 end-to-end latency = 120ms, p99 = 300ms for single-request text generation jobs (average prompt ~120 tokens).
- Peak concurrency today: ~120 concurrent requests; expected growth to ~400 in 6 months.
- Typical traffic pattern: short bursts (1-2 min) followed by steady background of 40-60 rps.
- Streaming requirements: must support token-level streaming to the browser for chat sessions (latency between tokens should be <50ms ideally).
- Current provider: reporting p95 ~220ms, p99 ~620ms (observed under current test harness).

Proposed qualification plan (next steps):
1) You share the request-size distribution and a short 24-hour synthetic trace (or our team can replay production-like traces if you can provide recent logs).
2) Redwood runs a POC with hosted API configured to match your concurrency and streaming workload (we'll run both steady-state and burst tests).
3) We'll produce a p95/p99 comparison report (end-to-end, including network and client-side streaming) and a recommended config (batching, KV cache, concurrency limits, quantization profile).

Action items for FinLytics:
- Please attach the SLO matrix you use internally (or confirm the numbers above).
- Share a representative 2-hour trace and an example prompt set.

I’ve attached a SLO matrix template and a short test-plan draft to make it easy.

Thanks — happy to jump on a quick alignment call if helpful.

Best,
Laura

Hi all —

Two quick technical notes from the runtime/serving side to help set expectations for the POC comparison: 

- End-to-end p95/p99: our hosted API includes network egress and CloudFront edge hops for customer traffic. For apples-to-apples comparison, please confirm whether FinLytics’ current numbers include client-side processing and network hops; if not, we’ll run both "server-only" and "end-to-end" measurements.

- Streaming behavior differences: some providers buffer token batches aggressively which reduces per-token overhead but increases perceived latency for first tokens. Redwood’s streaming path is optimized for sub-token flushes and can trade off slightly higher server-side CPU for lower token-to-token latency.

- Concurrency handling: to hit consistent p99 at high concurrency we typically tune a combination of batching window (ms), KV cache warmup, and worker concurrency. We’ll include the configuration we used during the POC so your team can reproduce results on Dedicated if you want to later.

Happy to hop on call to walk through the test-plan details.

—Marissa
Marissa Cole | Solutions Architect, Redwood Inference
